passage:
"Pema, give me five lemons," Sarika Aunty said at her vegetable stall.
Pema, five, counted, touching each one. "One, two, three, four, five."
"Good. Now, who has more, you or me?" Aunty held up three.
Pema looked. "Me! Five is more."
"How many more?"
Pema pointed at her lemons, then at Aunty's. She pushed her extra two to the side. "Two more!"
"Clever girl. Now give one to me."
"Now I have four, you have four! Same!"
"Same. So who gets the free guava?"
Pema grinned. "Both!"

qa.q: How many lemons did Sarika Aunty ask for?
qa.a: Five lemons.

qa.q: How did Pema feel when she said 'Same!'?
qa.a: Pema felt excited and proud, noticing the numbers had become equal.

qa.q: How did Sarika Aunty turn the sale into a counting lesson?
qa.a: She asked who had more and how many more, and let Pema move lemons to see equal amounts.

qa.q: How might Sarika Aunty feel when Pema says 'Both!'?
qa.a: Sarika Aunty probably felt amused and happy at Pema's clever answer.

grounding: At a vegetable stall, a five-year-old counts and compares quantities with a shopkeeper.

passage: Kindergarten note, Pongal week. We gave each child sugarcane pieces at snack time. Karthik (5) had four; his friend Ravi had six. Karthik counted both piles twice, frowned, and said, "Ravi has more. Two more." Last month he would have said "same", because his pieces looked long. I asked what would make it fair. He moved one of Ravi's pieces to his own pile. "Now five and five." Ravi agreed. I'll send home a counting game for the holidays. — Abhinav Sir

qa.q: How many pieces did Karthik have?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he frowned at the piles?
qa.a: Karthik felt it was unfair and a little annoyed that Ravi had more.

qa.q: How did Abhinav Sir build on Karthik's counting?
qa.a: He asked what would make it fair, letting Karthik move pieces to make equal piles.

qa.q: How might Ravi feel about giving up a piece?
qa.a: Ravi agreed, so he probably felt fine, perhaps happy that it was fair.

grounding: A Pongal-week kindergarten note records a five-year-old counting to compare more and less.

passage: At Baisakhi harvest in their village near Ludhiana, Jasleen tied wheat into bundles while her son Lokesh, five, sat on the cart. "Count them for me," she called. Lokesh pointed. "One, two, three… eleven!" He had skipped seven. Jasleen laughed. "Again, slowly. Touch each one." This time he touched every bundle and got twelve. "Mamma, that side has more than this side!" "How do you know?" "Because this side is only five." Jasleen tossed him a sugarcane stick. "My accountant."

qa.q: How many bundles did Lokesh count the second time?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt when Jasleen called him 'My accountant'?
qa.a: Lokesh probably felt proud and pleased at the praise.

qa.q: What tip helped Lokesh count correctly?
qa.a: Counting slowly and touching each bundle, so he didn't skip any.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel as Lokesh compares the two sides?
qa.a: Jasleen probably feels amused and proud, seeing him understand more and less.

grounding: At a village harvest, a five-year-old learns to count carefully and compare quantities.

passage: In their Hyderabad flat, Gopika Aunty from next door was draining rice when Asif, five, asked for her old colander. She gave it to him. He put it on his head. "Astronaut helmet!" Then he held it up to the window. "Look, the sun has holes!" He poured water through it over his toy elephant. "Rain shower." Then he tapped it with a spoon. "Drum!" Gopika Aunty lost count of what it became. When she asked for it back, it was a boat full of marbles.

qa.q: What did Asif first call the colander?
qa.a: An astronaut helmet.

qa.q: How was Asif feeling as he found use after use?
qa.a: Asif felt excited and playful, delighted with each new idea.

qa.q: How could Gopika Aunty encourage Asif's imaginative thinking?
qa.a: Give him safe everyday objects and ask 'What else could it be?' instead of telling him.

qa.q: How might Gopika Aunty feel asking for her colander back?
qa.a: She probably felt amused and impressed that it had become a boat full of marbles.

grounding: A five-year-old invents many uses for an old kitchen colander.

passage:
"Power's gone again," Vishal, eight, groaned. The monsoon rain drummed on the roof.
Usha, five, switched on the torch. "Look! A rabbit." She made ears with her fingers on the wall.
"That's a bad rabbit."
"It's a rabbit that lost his ears in the rain." She wiggled her fingers. "Now it's a crab. Now a rain monster!"
"What does the rain monster eat?"
"Umbrellas. And your homework."
Vishal laughed. "Okay, what if the torch is a lighthouse?"
Usha shone it at the ceiling. "Boats, come home!"

qa.q: What was the first shadow Usha made?
qa.a: A rabbit.

qa.q: How was Usha feeling as she changed the shadow from rabbit to crab to monster?
qa.a: Usha felt playful and excited, enjoying inventing new ideas.

qa.q: How did Vishal help the game grow?
qa.a: He asked questions and added his own 'what if', like the torch as a lighthouse.

qa.q: How might Vishal's mood change during the game?
qa.a: Vishal went from grumpy about the power cut to laughing and joining in.

grounding: During a monsoon power cut, a five-year-old invents shadow creatures and stories with her brother.

passage: Classroom note, the week before Christmas. We had a pile of used paper cups left from the party. I asked the children, "What could these be?" Most said "cups". Anand (5) said, "Bells!" and hung two on a string. Then, "A telephone," joining two with thread. Then he stacked them: "A tower for the snowman's cat." By the end he had invented seven uses, and others began copying. Tomorrow I'll bring a box of clean junk and let them invent freely. — Thomas

qa.q: How many uses did Anand invent?
qa.a: Seven uses.

qa.q: How might Anand have felt as others began copying him?
qa.a: Anand probably felt proud and excited that his ideas caught on.

qa.q: What is Thomas planning, and why will it help?
qa.a: Bringing a box of clean junk for free inventing, to give all the children more chances to think of new uses.

qa.q: How might the other children see Anand's ideas?
qa.a: They probably found them fun and inspiring, which is why they started copying.

grounding: A teacher's Christmas-week note records a five-year-old inventing many uses for paper cups.

passage:
Monday. At circle time, Nandini, five, keeps squeezing between friends and bumping elbows. Tina cries, "She's too close!"
Wednesday. Indu Ma'am teaches "bubble space": arms out, turn slowly, don't pop anyone's bubble. Nandini spins carefully, giggling, and shifts back.
Friday. During musical statues, Nandini runs, stops, wobbles, but keeps her balance and her space. When she wants to hug Tina, she asks first. Tina says no. Nandini nods and hugs her teddy instead.

qa.q: What does Indu Ma'am teach on Wednesday?
qa.a: Bubble space.

qa.q: What might Nandini have felt when Tina said no to the hug?
qa.a: Nandini was probably a little disappointed but accepted it calmly.

qa.q: How did 'bubble space' help Nandini?
qa.a: Stretching her arms and turning showed her how much room others need, so she stopped bumping.

qa.q: How might Tina feel when Nandini asks before hugging?
qa.a: Tina probably felt respected and safe, able to say no.

grounding: Over a week, a five-year-old learns personal space, balance in games and asking before hugging.

passage: The lane outside their Goa house was crowded and slippery on Holi afternoon, and Lalit, five, was covered in green. His friend Maria from the next house had come out in a new white frock. Lalit ran at her with a fistful of colour, slipped on the wet tiles, and caught himself on the gate. Maria stepped back. "No colour on me! Stop!" Lalit stopped, fist still raised. He looked at her frock. Then he rubbed the colour on his own cheeks instead. "Okay. Only me." Maria laughed.

qa.q: What was Maria wearing?
qa.a: A new white frock.

qa.q: What might Lalit have felt when Maria said stop?
qa.a: Lalit was probably disappointed for a moment, but chose to respect her.

qa.q: What did Lalit get right, and how can adults reinforce it?
qa.a: He stopped the moment Maria said no and put the colour on himself; adults can praise him for listening to 'stop'.

qa.q: How might Maria feel when Lalit stops?
qa.a: Maria probably felt relieved and respected, and laughed.

grounding: On a crowded Holi afternoon, a five-year-old keeps his balance and honours a friend's 'stop'.

passage: At the Christmas party in their Bengaluru apartment clubhouse, the children played musical chairs. Kiran, six, loved to win. When the music stopped, he dived for a chair and nearly knocked Uma off. "Ow! You pushed me!" Kiran froze. The uncle running the game paused the music. Kiran looked at Uma rubbing her arm. "Sorry. I'll wait for my own chair." Next round he ran, stopped, balanced on one foot, and sat only when there was an empty seat.

qa.q: What game did the children play?
qa.a: Musical chairs.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when he froze?
qa.a: Kiran felt startled and sorry after hurting Uma.

qa.q: How did Kiran change his play after pushing Uma?
qa.a: He apologised and then only sat on an empty chair, controlling his body and keeping his space.

qa.q: How might Uma feel after Kiran's apology?
qa.a: Uma probably felt better and more willing to keep playing.

grounding: At a Christmas party game, a six-year-old learns to control his body and respect a friend's space.

passage: I'm Rafiq, and I live in the flat opposite Bidisha's. For two weeks I watched her fall off her small cycle in our compound, again and again, after her father took the side wheels off. She's five. Yesterday she pedalled all the way to the gate without falling. She stopped, put one foot down, and looked round to see who had seen. Then she walked the cycle back very slowly, chin up, shoulders back, like a queen. I clapped. She pretended not to care, but she was smiling.

qa.q: What did Bidisha's father take off her cycle?
qa.a: The side wheels.

qa.q: What might Bidisha have felt walking back with her chin up?
qa.a: Bidisha probably felt proud and satisfied after finally riding to the gate.

qa.q: How could adults support Bidisha's pride in her effort?
qa.a: Praise her practice and not giving up after falls, not just the result.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see Bidisha's success?
qa.a: Rafiq is pleased and amused, clapping and noticing she was smiling even while pretending not to care.

grounding: A neighbour watches a five-year-old stand taller with pride after learning to ride without side wheels.

passage:
Ten days before Ganesh Chaturthi, Pradeep, five, tried to shape a small clay Ganpati with his mother, Lakshmi. The trunk fell off. He squashed the whole thing and cried.
Five days later, he tried again, patting slowly. The ears were uneven, but the trunk stayed on.
On festival morning, his little Ganpati sat beside the big one on the altar. When his Mama visited, Pradeep stood very straight and said, "I made that one. By myself. Mostly."

qa.q: What fell off Pradeep's first clay Ganpati?
qa.a: The trunk.

qa.q: What does Pradeep standing very straight on festival morning show?
qa.a: Pradeep felt proud of making the Ganpati himself.

qa.q: How could Lakshmi encourage healthy pride?
qa.a: Praise his patience in trying again and his honest 'mostly', not just how it looks.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's Mama feel hearing 'By myself. Mostly'?
qa.a: Mama would likely feel charmed and amused by his pride and honesty.

grounding: Before Ganesh Chaturthi, a five-year-old moves from frustration to pride in his own clay idol.

passage: Sports day at Nilesh's school fell on the hottest April morning, and the sack race started late. Nilesh, six, had practised with a rice sack at home with his sister Kashish. Halfway, he tripped and fell flat. Other children passed him. He struggled up, hopped on, and crossed the line fourth, red-faced and dusty. He didn't win a medal. But when Kashish ran to him, he said, "I fell and I didn't stop!" and stood tall, holding the sack like a flag.

qa.q: Which place did Nilesh finish in?
qa.a: Fourth.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel crossing the line fourth?
qa.a: Nilesh felt proud of himself for getting up and finishing, even without a medal.

qa.q: How could Kashish support Nilesh's pride?
qa.a: Praise his getting up and finishing, the part he is proudest of.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel seeing him stand tall with the sack?
qa.a: Kashish would likely feel proud and happy, having practised with him.

grounding: On a hot sports day, a six-year-old feels proud of finishing a race after falling.

passage: During story time in the kindergarten, Jomon, five, didn't reach the toilet in time. Someone giggled. Jomon stood frozen, face hot, then hid under the table with his knees pulled up. "I'm a bad boy," he whispered. Jyoti Ma'am crouched beside him, blocking the others' view. "You're not bad. Your body was in a hurry. It happens to everyone." She quietly took him to change into spare shorts. Back in class, she asked him to hand out the crayons.

qa.q: Where did Jomon hide?
qa.a: Under the table.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he whispered 'I'm a bad boy'?
qa.a: Jomon felt ashamed, as if the accident made him bad.

qa.q: How did Jyoti Ma'am respond to Jomon's shame?
qa.a: She blocked the others' view, told him he wasn't bad, changed him quietly, and gave him a helpful job to restore his dignity.

qa.q: How might the child who giggled feel after Jyoti Ma'am's calm response?
qa.a: That child might feel a bit embarrassed and learn that accidents are normal, not funny.

grounding: In kindergarten, a five-year-old feels ashamed after a toilet accident and his teacher responds with kindness.

passage: I'm Santosh, and I was running the sound at our colony's Diwali programme. Rashmi, six, came on stage to recite a poem. After the second line she stopped. Her face went blank. Then someone in the front row laughed. She put her hands over her face and ran off the stage. I heard her tell her mother, "I'm stupid. Everyone saw." Her mother hugged her. "You're not stupid. You forgot. Let's say the poem at home, just for Papa." I don't know what she felt inside, but she didn't come back out.

qa.q: What was Rashmi reciting?
qa.a: A poem.

qa.q: What might Rashmi have been feeling when she said 'I'm stupid'?
qa.a: Rashmi probably felt deeply ashamed, as if forgetting made her stupid.

qa.q: How did Rashmi's mother respond helpfully?
qa.a: She hugged her, separated the mistake from who Rashmi is, and offered a safe, small audience at home.

qa.q: How does Santosh see the moment?
qa.a: Santosh saw what happened and heard her words, but admits not knowing how she felt inside.

grounding: At a Diwali programme, a neighbour sees a six-year-old feel ashamed after forgetting her poem, and her mother comfort her.

passage:
December 20. Thomas, five, dropped the little clay shepherd from the Christmas crib, and its head broke off. He hid it in his pocket and wouldn't eat dinner. When his father, Kamal, asked, he burst into tears. "I break everything. I'm a bad boy."
December 21. Kamal sat with him. "You're a good boy who broke a shepherd. Let's fix it." They glued the head on together.
Christmas Eve. Thomas placed the mended shepherd in the crib himself, carefully, and showed Grandma the crack.

qa.q: What broke off the clay shepherd?
qa.a: Its head.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when he said 'I'm a bad boy'?
qa.a: Thomas felt ashamed, believing the accident meant he was bad.

qa.q: How did Kamal help Thomas move past shame?
qa.a: He separated the mistake from who Thomas is and fixed the shepherd together with him.

qa.q: How might Grandma feel when Thomas shows her the crack?
qa.a: Grandma would likely feel touched that he is proud of mending it rather than hiding it.

grounding: Over the Christmas season, a five-year-old moves from shame over a broken crib figure to repairing it with his father.

passage: I'm Farhan, and I was watering my plants when Ritu, five, kicked her ball into the pot on my balcony. It cracked, and the tulsi fell over. She ran. Ten minutes later my doorbell rang. Ritu stood there with her mother, looking at her feet. "I broke your pot," she said very quietly. "I'm sorry." She held out her piggy bank. I told her she didn't need to pay, but she could help me replant the tulsi. She dug so carefully. I don't know exactly what she felt, but she kept saying sorry.

qa.q: What plant fell over?
qa.a: The tulsi.

qa.q: What might Ritu have felt standing at the door, looking at her feet?
qa.a: Ritu probably felt guilty and sorry for breaking the pot.

qa.q: How did Farhan help Ritu make amends?
qa.a: He accepted the apology, refused the money, and let her help replant the tulsi.

qa.q: How does Farhan see Ritu's apology?
qa.a: Farhan is touched by it, noticing her care in replanting, while admitting not knowing exactly what she felt.

grounding: A neighbour describes a five-year-old returning to confess and make amends for breaking a flowerpot.

passage:
Holi morning. Hrithik, six, sprayed his water gun wildly and soaked his brother Deepak's library book, left on the steps. The pages went pink. Hrithik hid the gun and said nothing.
That night. Hrithik couldn't sleep. He crept to Deepak's bed. "I did the book. Sorry." Deepak groaned, then said, "Thanks for telling."
Two days later. Hrithik went with Deepak to the library, holding his hand, and told the librarian himself. He gave his saved coins towards a new copy.

qa.q: What colour did the pages go?
qa.a: Pink.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when he couldn't sleep?
qa.a: Hrithik felt guilty about ruining the book and hiding it.

qa.q: How did Hrithik make things right?
qa.a: He told Deepak, went to the librarian himself, and gave his saved coins towards a new copy.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel when Hrithik confesses at night?
qa.a: Deepak was annoyed but also appreciative that Hrithik told the truth.

grounding: Over Holi week, a six-year-old moves from hiding a mistake to confessing and making amends.

passage: It was pouring on the way home from school, and Harish, five, had forgotten his umbrella. His friend Chetan lent him his new blue one. At the bus stop, Harish put it down to watch a dog, and when the bus came, he forgot it. Chetan walked home soaked. Next morning Harish saw him sneezing and felt his stomach twist. He went straight to him. "I lost your umbrella. It was my fault. Sorry." Then he asked his Amma if they could buy a new one.

qa.q: What colour was Chetan's umbrella?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when his stomach twisted?
qa.a: Harish felt guilty, seeing Chetan sneezing because of the lost umbrella.

qa.q: How did Harish handle his mistake?
qa.a: He told Chetan it was his fault, said sorry, and asked Amma to help replace it.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel hearing the apology?
qa.a: Chetan might still be annoyed about getting wet but likely feels better hearing Harish own up.

grounding: On a rainy monsoon day, a five-year-old feels guilty for losing a friend's umbrella and owns up.

passage:
Parul's fifth birthday. When the whole family sang loudly and everyone looked at her, Parul hid her face in Papa's shirt and wouldn't blow out the candles. Pranav blew them with her, quietly.
A week later, at a cousin's party. Parul watched the birthday girl clap along. "She's not shy," Parul whispered.
A month later, at another cousin's birthday. When they sang, Parul stood at the side, shy but smiling, and sang softly, not looking at anyone.

qa.q: Who blew out the candles with Parul?
qa.a: Papa, Pranav.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when she hid her face in Papa's shirt?
qa.a: Parul felt embarrassed and overwhelmed by everyone singing and looking at her.

qa.q: How did Pranav help Parul through the moment?
qa.a: He didn't force her; he quietly helped blow out the candles, taking the spotlight off her.

qa.q: How might the family feel seeing Parul hide?
qa.a: They might feel surprised and gentle, realising the attention was too much for her.

grounding: Over a month of birthdays, a five-year-old moves from hiding in embarrassment to joining in shyly.

passage: The Christmas concert had already started when Francis, five, discovered his angel wings were tied on backwards, and there was no time to fix them. He walked on stage anyway. The audience laughed kindly at the crooked wings. Francis turned red, stared at the floor, and stopped singing. Manoj Sir, at the piano, caught his eye, pointed at his own wonky tie, and winked. Francis gave a tiny smile. He sang the last verse softly, then ran off to hide behind the curtain.

qa.q: What was wrong with Francis's wings?
qa.a: They were tied on backwards.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when he turned red and stared at the floor?
qa.a: Francis felt embarrassed by the unexpected laughter and attention.

qa.q: How did Manoj Sir help Francis without drawing more attention?
qa.a: He caught his eye, pointed at his own wonky tie and winked, showing that mistakes are okay.

qa.q: How might the audience see Francis?
qa.a: The audience probably found him sweet and didn't mean to embarrass him.

grounding: At a rushed Christmas concert, a five-year-old is embarrassed by laughter and his teacher quietly helps.

passage: On Diwali evening, Sahil's Delhi flat filled with relatives. Every aunty pinched his cheeks and said, "So big now! Say a poem!" Sahil, five, felt everyone looking. His ears went hot. He hid behind the curtain and wouldn't come out. His Dadi, Sharmila, came and sat on the floor beside the curtain. "Too many eyes?" He nodded. "Stay with me. You can say the poem to just me, later." Sahil peeked out, then leaned against her shoulder.

qa.q: What did every aunty say?
qa.a: So big now! Say a poem!

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when his ears went hot?
qa.a: Sahil felt embarrassed and overwhelmed by all the attention.

qa.q: How did Dadi help Sahil?
qa.a: She sat with him, named the feeling, and offered a smaller audience later instead of forcing him.

qa.q: How might the aunties feel when Sahil hides?
qa.a: They might be a little disappointed or amused, not realising the attention was too much for him.

grounding: On Diwali evening, a five-year-old is overwhelmed by relatives' attention and his grandmother gives him space.

passage:
Monday. Arohi, five, noticed her Ammamma, Rukmini, lying down in the afternoon, which she never did. Arohi stood in the doorway, quiet, holding her doll.
Tuesday. Ammamma coughed a lot. Arohi brought her a glass of water without being asked and patted her hand. "Ammamma, sad?" "Just tired, kanna."
Friday. Ammamma sat in the garden again. Arohi drew her a picture of a sun with a smiling face and said, "For your cough to go away."

qa.q: What did Arohi bring Ammamma on Tuesday?
qa.a: A glass of water.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling standing quietly in the doorway?
qa.a: Arohi felt worried and sad to see Ammamma lying down, which she never did.

qa.q: How could the family support Arohi's sympathy?
qa.a: Let her help in small ways, like bringing water, and explain simply how Ammamma is feeling.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel receiving the sun picture?
qa.a: Rukmini would likely feel touched and loved by Arohi's care.

grounding: Over a week, a five-year-old shows growing concern and sympathy for her unwell grandmother.

passage: The Holi party in the park was loud and crowded, and Vandana, five, got colour in her eyes. She screamed and rubbed them, crying. The grown-ups were far off near the music. Sunaina, six, stopped throwing colour at once. Her face crumpled too. She took Vandana's hand and shouted, "Mamma! Help!" until her mother came running with a water bottle. While Vandana's eyes were rinsed, Sunaina stroked her back and kept saying, "It's okay, it's okay."

qa.q: Where were the grown-ups?
qa.a: Far off near the music.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling when her face crumpled?
qa.a: Sunaina felt worried and sad for Vandana, sharing her distress.

qa.q: What did Sunaina do that helped?
qa.a: She stopped playing, held Vandana's hand, called loudly for an adult, and comforted her.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel with Sunaina stroking her back?
qa.a: Vandana was probably frightened but comforted, knowing her friend was there.

grounding: At a noisy Holi party, a six-year-old feels sympathy for a hurt friend and calls an adult for help.

passage: On a foggy January morning in their Lucknow colony, Charu, five, found a puppy shivering under a parked scooter. It whimpered. Charu's lip trembled. "It's cold. It's crying." She pulled off her own woollen cap and tried to put it on the puppy. Farida Aunty from next door saw and came over with an old towel and a bowl of warm milk. "You noticed it was sad. That was kind." Charu crouched close, watching the puppy lap, and wouldn't leave until it stopped shaking.

qa.q: Where was the puppy?
qa.a: Under a parked scooter.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when her lip trembled?
qa.a: Charu felt sad and worried for the shivering puppy.

qa.q: How did Farida Aunty support Charu's sympathy?
qa.a: She helped with a towel and warm milk, and named Charu's kindness.

qa.q: How might Farida Aunty feel seeing Charu offer her own cap?
qa.a: Farida Aunty probably felt touched by Charu's kindness.

grounding: On a foggy winter morning, a five-year-old feels sympathy for a shivering puppy and a neighbour helps.

passage:
Monday. At the playground, Avni, five, fell and scraped her knee. Ritu, also five, stared, then ran off to the swings.
Wednesday. Avni still had the bandage. Ritu looked at it for a long time, then patted it gently. "Does it hurt?" "A bit."
Friday. When a younger boy tripped near the slide and started crying, Ritu ran to him first, knelt, and said, "Blow on it. Like this." Then she fetched the teacher.

qa.q: What happened to Avni on Monday?
qa.a: She fell and scraped her knee.

qa.q: What might Ritu have felt when she ran off on Monday?
qa.a: Ritu was probably startled and unsure what to do on seeing Avni hurt.

qa.q: What did Ritu do on Friday that showed growing concern?
qa.a: She ran to the boy first, comforted him by blowing on the hurt, and fetched the teacher.

qa.q: How might the younger boy feel when Ritu kneels beside him?
qa.a: He probably felt comforted and less alone in his pain.

grounding: Over a week, a five-year-old moves from avoiding a friend's injury to comforting a hurt child and getting help.

passage: The school's winter picnic at Lodhi Garden was noisy, and Elizabeth Ma'am was busy counting heads when a bee stung Rimjhim on the hand. She wailed. Vasudha, five, heard her and dropped her sandwich. She sat beside Rimjhim, held her other hand, and blew on the sting. "I'll get Ma'am." She pushed through the crowd, tugged Elizabeth Ma'am's sleeve, and pointed. When Ma'am came with the first-aid bag, Vasudha stayed close, stroking Rimjhim's hair.

qa.q: What stung Rimjhim?
qa.a: A bee.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she dropped her sandwich?
qa.a: Vasudha felt worried and concerned for Rimjhim.

qa.q: How did Vasudha comfort Rimjhim and get help?
qa.a: She held her hand, blew on the sting, fetched Elizabeth Ma'am, and stayed beside her.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth Ma'am feel about Vasudha's help?
qa.a: Elizabeth Ma'am likely felt grateful and proud that Vasudha fetched her quickly and stayed kind.

grounding: At a noisy winter picnic, a five-year-old notices a friend's pain, comforts her and fetches the teacher.

passage: While hanging Diwali lights on the balcony of their Pune flat, Yogesh pinched his finger in the ladder and said, "Ouch!" loudly. Manjula, five, looked up from her rangoli. Papa was shaking his hand, face screwed up. She ran inside, came back with her toy doctor set, and pressed the plastic stethoscope to his finger. "Papa, blow." She blew on it herself. Then she kissed the finger. "Better?" Yogesh laughed. "Much better, Doctor Manjula."

qa.q: What was Yogesh hanging on the balcony?
qa.a: Diwali lights.

qa.q: What might Manjula have felt seeing Papa's screwed-up face?

passage: It was almost bedtime, and Reena, six, was one move from winning ludo when Anjali, her mother, cut her last token. Reena's face went red. She swept the board, and pieces flew. "Not fair!" Anjali didn't shout. "You're really cross. Let's do dragon breaths." Reena breathed out hard three times, like fire. Her fists opened. "Can we play once more tomorrow?" "Yes. And you can pick up the pieces now." Grumbling a little, Reena picked them up.

passage: In the week before Christmas in Aizawl, Lalremsiami, five, spent all afternoon cutting a paper star. When she pulled it off the table, one point tore. She threw the scissors down and stamped her foot, tears coming. Rukmini Aunty, her neighbour, watched from the doorway and waited. Lalremsiami hugged her knees and hummed a carol under her breath, rocking. After a minute she wiped her face and said, "I'll stick it." She taped the point back on, crooked, and hung it anyway.

qa.q: What tore on Lalremsiami's star?
qa.a: One point.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she stamped her foot?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt frustrated and upset that her star tore after all her work.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do to soothe herself?
qa.a: She hugged her knees, hummed a carol and rocked, then chose to fix the star with tape.

qa.q: How might Rukmini Aunty feel watching from the doorway?
qa.a: Rukmini Aunty probably felt impressed and relieved that Lalremsiami calmed herself without help.

grounding: In the week before Christmas, a five-year-old recovers from a torn paper star by soothing herself.

passage:
"I lost again!" Hafsa, five, pushed the carrom striker away. Rain had kept them inside all week.
"You nearly got the queen," said Kashish, her big sister.
"I never win!" Hafsa's chin wobbled.
"Want to throw the cushion first?"
Hafsa threw it at the wall. Thump. Then she sat on it. "Still cross."
"Okay. Count the raindrops on the window with me. Ten."
Hafsa counted slowly. By seven she was smiling.
"Again?"
"Only if I go first."
"Deal."

qa.q: What had kept them inside all week?
qa.a: Rain.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when her chin wobbled?
qa.a: Hafsa felt frustrated and disappointed at losing again.

qa.q: How did Kashish help Hafsa recover?
qa.a: She offered a safe way to let out anger, then a calm counting activity, and a fair next game.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel when Hafsa asks to play again?
qa.a: Kashish probably felt pleased and relieved that her sister bounced back.

grounding: During a rainy week indoors, a big sister helps a five-year-old recover from losing at carrom.
